**Question:** If an import file begins with a byte-order mark — the invisible marker that spreadsheet programs and some Windows editors add to the front of a UTF-8 file — should the import skip it and read the file normally, or treat it as part of the first field and fail?

Why it matters: Read strictly, that marker becomes part of the first column name, so a file that looks perfectly correct in an editor is rejected with status 2 and a confusing "wrong header" message. This is the single most common way a hand-edited export file fails to import.

**Recommended:** Option A - Consistent with the previous answer about quoted headers: a file that round-trips through a spreadsheet should import. It is also a smaller change than the error path it avoids — the file is simply opened with the encoding variant that discards a leading marker, for both file shapes.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Skip it. A single leading byte-order mark is discarded before parsing, for both the table and the structured shape; everything after it is read as UTF-8 as normal. |
| B | Fail. The marker is data like any other, so it corrupts the first column name (table) or the document's first character (structured) and the import fails with status 2. |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
